title: Forward guidance and market repricing
method: Each release carries the rate direction explicitly contemplated after the announced decision. A hold or two-sided signal requires affirmative evidence. Unspecified guidance remains a separate category. Conditional language can identify a direction without promising a move.

Match the institution, release date and type of communication. The US sample uses the FOMC statement window. The ECB decision release and subsequent conference have separate windows, including the questions to the ECB President. Each release has equal weight within its own cell.

A positive rate change means yields or expected rates rose. Rates are in basis points and stock index returns in percent. A median difference subtracts the easing-group median from the tightening-group median within the same window and action filter. A blank requires a missing observation or comparison. An observed zero counts as zero.

These are selected historical releases. Dates in the same policy cycle can share expectations and economic conditions. Even unchanged policy can surprise, and forecasts, asset purchases and economic news can accompany a statement. The comparisons describe repricing and do not identify the independent effect of the words.

A change in guidance compares two verified consecutive decisions with comparable communications. Gaps stay unclassified. Moving into or out of unspecified guidance changes explicitness. Only transitions between explicit states receive a direction.

banks.name: Federal Reserve

windows.label: Decision release
windows.definition: 10 min before to 20 min after the statement.

events.evidence: Even with productivity improving, policymakers thought spending might grow faster than potential supply and increase inflation pressure.
The Committee again judged demand growth excessive relative to supply and identified inflation as the predominant risk.
Demand still exceeded rapid productivity-driven supply gains, and pressure on resources warranted a larger increase.
Demand appeared to be slowing toward potential, but tight resource use still left inflation as the main concern.
Moderating demand and productivity gains helped reconcile growth with supply. Tight labor markets still posed an inflation risk.
Demand growth had moderated; unusually high resource utilization and energy costs still threatened price stability.
A tight labor market and higher energy prices coexisted with softening spending and tighter financial conditions.
Energy costs, deteriorating confidence and earnings shortfalls had shifted the predominant economic risk toward weakness.
With sales and production weakening, the Committee cut between scheduled meetings and retained a downside economic-risk assessment.
Eroding confidence and expensive energy reinforced weakness in demand. Inflation pressures remained contained.
The attacks intensified uncertainty against an already weak backdrop for employment, output and investment.
Economic activity remained soft, and underlying inflation could edge lower. The Committee continued to see greater risks of economic weakness.
Signs of recovery had become more common, but the strength of final demand remained uncertain and downside economic risks persisted.
The Committee judged the risks to sustainable growth and price stability balanced as economic activity expanded.
Weak financial markets and uncertainty had prolonged the slowdown in demand, leaving the economic risk tilted toward weakness.
After lowering the target, the Committee judged risks to its two economic objectives broadly balanced.
The existing accommodative setting and productivity growth provided support, and risks to both objectives remained balanced.
Oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty were restraining spending and hiring; the Committee still viewed the overall economic risks as balanced.
The Committee judged geopolitical uncertainty too great to characterize the balance of risks reliably and emphasized close monitoring.
Growth risks appeared balanced, but a further fall from already low inflation was more likely than an increase.
The Committee cut the target to 1%. Downside inflation risk still predominated despite broadly even growth risks.
With inflation unusually low and substantial slack, the Committee expected accommodation could persist for an extended time.
Firmer spending had not prevented the labor market from weakening. The Committee again saw scope to maintain accommodation for an extended time.
Spending was firming and employment appeared to be stabilizing, but subdued prices still supported a prolonged accommodative setting.
The risk of declining inflation was closer to that of rising inflation. Low inflation and slack still justified maintaining accommodation for an extended time.
The Committee said it could wait before withdrawing accommodation, placing an eventual withdrawal on the prospective policy path.
Solid output growth and modest hiring gains left room for patience before removing accommodation.
With inflation low but incoming readings firmer, the Committee described a gradual pace for withdrawing accommodation.
Even after raising the target the Committee saw policy as accommodative and expected gradual further withdrawal, subject to the outlook.
The Committee still saw gradual removal of accommodation as appropriate despite balanced risks to growth and price stability.
After raising the target to 4.25%, the Committee expected some further gradual tightening to keep economic risks in balance.
After lifting the rate to 5.25%, the Committee explicitly contemplated additional firming, with its timing and extent dependent on growth and inflation.
The Committee kept 5.25% as growth moderated, but it still identified additional firming as the potential next adjustment.
The Committee still saw some inflation risk and singled out possible further firming, conditional on the outlook.
Although the Committee highlighted the danger that inflation might not moderate, its policy paragraph made future adjustments dependent on growth and inflation without specifying their direction.
The half-point cut was intended to cushion the economy against tightening credit. The Committee would reassess financial conditions and respond as needed.
Following another cut, the Committee saw the risks of higher inflation and weaker growth as roughly offsetting and offered a contingent response to subsequent developments.
Deteriorating market conditions and housing activity prompted a quarter-point cut. Future action remained contingent on the outlook.
An intermeeting cut addressed a deteriorating outlook and tighter credit. The Committee remained ready to respond promptly to downside growth risks.
The rate was cut to 3% amid financial stress and tighter credit. Downside risks remained after earlier policy actions.
The Committee cut to 2.25% as the outlook weakened, while acknowledging that the inflation outlook had also become more uncertain.
A quarter-point reduction brought the rate to 2%. The Committee noted both subdued spending and higher commodity prices and inflation expectations.
The target remained 2%. Downside growth risks appeared somewhat smaller while upside risks to inflation and expectations had increased.
The Committee held at 2% and remained concerned about both financial stress and uncertainty around inflation.
At the 2% hold, downside growth risks and upside inflation risks were both significant. The Committee said it would monitor financial developments and act as needed.
In the coordinated response, the US Committee cut to 1.5%. Deteriorating activity and falling commodity prices had reduced upside inflation risks.
The Committee reduced the target to 1% and saw remaining downside growth risks even after earlier policy and liquidity measures.
The Committee replaced the 1% point target with a 0–0.25% range and expected economic weakness to justify very low rates for some time.
The Committee maintained the 0–0.25% range and expected exceptionally low rates to remain warranted for a period of time.
The Committee maintained 0–0.25% and explicitly expected exceptionally low rates to be needed for a prolonged period.
Slack, subdued inflation and stable expectations were expected to justify an extended period of exceptionally low rates.
The Committee retained its extended low-rate horizon and indicated readiness to offer additional accommodation if required.
The 0–0.25% range and extended low-rate guidance remained. The additional easing came through securities purchases.
The Committee placed a date on its low-rate outlook, expecting exceptionally low rates to remain warranted at least through mid-2013.
The Committee reaffirmed its expectation of very low rates at least through mid-2013 as it recognized downside risks to activity.
The Committee expected exceptionally low rates at least through mid-2015 and accommodation to continue even after activity strengthened.
The low rate was expected to persist while unemployment exceeded 6.5%, the one-to-two-year inflation projection did not exceed 2.5% and longer-run expectations stayed anchored.
The Committee expected the range to stay near zero well after unemployment fell below 6.5%, particularly if projected inflation remained below target.
The Committee anticipated retaining the near-zero range for a considerable time after the asset purchase program ended, especially with below-target projected inflation and anchored expectations.
The Committee judged it could wait before beginning policy normalization and explicitly regarded this as consistent with its earlier low-rate holding guidance.
The first move raised the range to 0.25–0.50%, and policymakers expected economic conditions to justify only gradual additional rate increases.
After a quarter-point increase, the Committee expected only gradual further rate rises and a rate below its longer-run level for a time.
The rate stayed at 1.00–1.25%. The Committee still expected the economy to justify a gradual increase in the funds rate.
After raising the range to 2.25–2.50%, the Committee judged that some further gradual increases would be consistent with continued expansion and near-target inflation.
The Committee said it would be patient in deciding which future rate adjustments were appropriate, citing global developments and muted inflation.
Increased uncertainty and subdued inflation led the Committee to emphasize readiness to act to sustain the expansion. It retained the current range.
The quarter-point reduction responded to global developments and muted inflation. Subsequent policy was left conditional on incoming information.
The Committee cut to 1.50–1.75% and said it would evaluate the appropriate future path in light of new information.
The coronavirus posed evolving risks to activity. The Committee made an intermeeting half-point cut and said it would use its tools to support the economy.
The Committee cut to 0–0.25% and expected to maintain this range until it was confident the economy had weathered the shock and was on course for its objectives.
The Committee retained the near-zero range and expected it to last until the economy had weathered the public-health shock and was on track toward its objectives.
The Committee expected to retain the near-zero range until maximum-employment conditions were reached and inflation had reached 2% and was on track to run moderately above it for a time.
The near-zero range was still expected to last until maximum-employment conditions and the stated inflation conditions were achieved.
With inflation already above 2% for a time, the Committee now tied maintaining the current rate range to reaching maximum-employment conditions.
Elevated inflation and a strong labor market led the Committee to explicitly anticipate that an increase in the range would soon be appropriate.
Liftoff took the range to 0.25–0.50%, and the Committee anticipated a continuing series of appropriate increases.
The Committee raised the range to 0.75–1.00% and continued to expect further increases, given high inflation and a strong labor market.
The Committee raised the range to 1.50–1.75% and still explicitly anticipated further increases as inflation remained elevated.
The rate rose to 2.25–2.50%. Despite softer spending and production indicators, the Committee still anticipated further increases.
The Committee raised the range to 3.00–3.25% and retained its expectation of further increases amid elevated inflation and a strong labor market.
The Committee raised the target and expected more increases to achieve sufficient restraint. It explicitly introduced cumulative tightening and policy lags into decisions about pace.
The half-point increase slowed the realized pace. Further increases were still expected to bring policy to a sufficiently restrictive setting.
The Committee raised the range by a quarter point and still anticipated further increases. It focused on their extent in light of previous tightening and transmission lags.
Following a quarter-point increase, the Committee judged further firming might be needed and acknowledged tighter credit conditions following banking strains.
Following the increase to 5.00–5.25%, the Committee would assess whether more firming was warranted, accounting for earlier tightening, lags and financial developments.
Holding at 5.00–5.25% bought time to assess additional information. The Committee still explicitly discussed the possible extent of further firming.
The Committee raised the range to 5.25–5.50% and retained its conditional language about whether additional firming would be warranted.
The Committee held the range and continued to frame the next directional option as possible additional firming, subject to cumulative tightening and lags.
The Committee judged that tighter financial and credit conditions could weigh on activity, while still specifically considering possible further firming.
The Committee added a qualifier when discussing whether any further firming might be appropriate. It still named that conditional upside option while leaving the rate unchanged.
The Committee kept 5.25–5.50%, dropped its description of potential further firming and identified greater confidence in lasting disinflation as a condition for reducing the rate.
The Committee again made a possible reduction conditional on greater confidence that inflation would return sustainably to 2%.
Recent inflation progress had stalled. The Committee kept its condition that greater confidence in sustained disinflation was necessary before reducing the rate.
The Committee saw modest renewed progress on inflation and still required greater confidence in sustained disinflation before a reduction was appropriate.
The Committee retained the disinflation-confidence hurdle for reducing the rate, while noting risks to both parts of its mandate.
The Committee cut the range by half a percentage point. Its prospective language now addressed possible further adjustments in generic, data-dependent terms.
The Committee lowered the range to 4.50–4.75% and conditioned further adjustments on the outlook, risks and incoming data.
The Committee reduced the range to 4.25–4.50% and placed the extent and timing of subsequent adjustments under review.
The Committee lowered the target to 3.75–4.00% and said further adjustments would depend on incoming evidence and risks.
The Committee cut to 3.50–3.75% and left the extent and timing of subsequent changes dependent on the data and outlook.
At 3.50–3.75%, the Committee left the timing and extent of further adjustments conditional on incoming information, the outlook and risks.
The Committee again made further rate adjustments conditional. It described the US implications of Middle East developments as uncertain and acknowledged risks to both objectives.
The adopted policy paragraph retained the generic reference to further adjustments even as higher global energy prices contributed to elevated inflation.
The unanimous statement held the range, identified sectoral supply shocks and reaffirmed the price-stability objective without describing the next funds-rate move.
The majority maintained the range and again emphasized above-goal inflation and supply shocks without stating an expected rate change.
The unanimous quarter-point increase took the range to 3.75–4.00%. The Committee said this action should speed the return to target and offered no subsequent move.
The Committee maintained 3.75–4.00% and said further information would help determine the appropriate stance. Activity was strong and inflation elevated.

examples.note: The funds target stayed at 1%. The Committee moved from a low-rate holding horizon to describing when it could withdraw accommodation. Compare this with December 2014, another hold that pointed to eventual tightening.

The Committee explicitly linked patience about eventual normalization to its earlier promise of sustained accommodation. The two-year yield fell in the statement window even as eventual tightening entered the guidance.

A reduction entered the statement as a conditional possibility. The Committee wanted greater confidence in sustained disinflation first. The next-meeting futures measure and the two-year yield both rose.
The Fed raised its target range by 25 basis points without specifying its next move. The current-meeting futures surprise separates the unexpected component from the announced adjustment.

nearPricedHolds.definition: Actual holds with an absolute current-meeting futures surprise (MP1) of at most 2 bp.

findings: Among rate holds the two-year Treasury median was -0.825 bp with explicit tightening guidance (12 releases) and +1.03 bp with easing guidance (5). The easing observations come from 2024.

Restricting holds to an absolute current-meeting futures surprise of 2 bp or less gives -0.19 bp for tightening (11) and +1.03 bp for easing (5). Even a well-anticipated current decision leaves room for news about later meetings.
Only 3 verified consecutive comparisons moved toward tightening and 1 toward easing. January 2004 and December 2014 both signalled eventual tightening at a hold and had opposite two-year yield moves.

banks.name: European Central Bank

windows.label: Decision release
windows.definition: Median quotes at 13:25–13:35 vs 14:00–14:10 Frankfurt time. From July 2022, 13:55–14:05 vs 14:30–14:40.

windows.label: Press conference
windows.definition: Median quotes at 14:15–14:25 vs 15:40–15:50 Frankfurt time. From July 2022, 14:30–14:40 vs 15:55–16:05.

events.evidence: Duisenberg reported unchanged rates, warned that higher prices must not feed wage and price setting, and declined to indicate a future rate bias when questioned.

The Council raised rates by a quarter point as monetary growth, credit and import prices increased inflation risks. Duisenberg asked listeners not to infer a directional bias from the size of the increase.
Trichet characterized the Council as particularly vigilant about upside inflation risks. In the questions that followed, he said a hike at the next meeting was possible but uncertain.
The Council increased all key rates by 25 basis points. Trichet said the Council had not decided this was the first of a series of increases and would watch inflation risks closely.

Draghi announced that the Council expected rates to remain at their existing levels or below them for an extended period, based on subdued inflation prospects, weak activity and muted monetary dynamics.
The Council expected key rates to remain at existing levels at least through summer 2019, and longer if needed to keep inflation on its expected sustained adjustment path.
The Council expected existing rates to persist at least through the first half of 2020 and longer if needed for sustained inflation convergence toward its then-prevailing aim.
The Council retained its first-half-2020 horizon but now expected rates to be at current levels or lower. It also asked committees to examine possible further accommodation.

The deposit rate fell to −0.50% while the other two rates stayed unchanged. The Council still expected rates to remain at current or lower levels until inflation convergence was convincing and visible in underlying inflation.

After adopting the symmetric 2% target, the Council expected rates at current or lower levels until inflation reached 2% well before the forecast horizon ended, persisted there and underlying inflation had advanced sufficiently.
The Council intended a quarter-point rise in July, expected another increase in September and allowed for a larger September step if the medium-term inflation outlook persisted or deteriorated.
The Council raised all three rates by half a point, larger than the June indication. It expected further normalization at upcoming meetings while moving to meeting-by-meeting calibration.
The Council raised rates by three quarters of a point and explicitly expected further increases over the next several meetings to restrain demand and prevent inflation expectations drifting upward.
With the deposit rate at 2.00% and medium-term inflation expected to stabilize at target, the Council committed to taking rate decisions meeting by meeting and disclaimed a pre-set path.

The Council left rates unchanged as the Middle East war raised near-term inflation and introduced downside growth risks. It would use the evolving outlook and transmission to judge the appropriate rate.
The Council kept the deposit rate at 2.00%. Higher energy costs worsened inflation risks while weakening economic sentiment, and the Council retained its meeting-by-meeting approach.

The Council raised the three rates by a quarter point while reiterating that it would determine the stance from incoming information rather than commit to a path. Staff projected headline inflation of 3.0% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027.
The Council kept the deposit rate at 2.25%. Energy prices were volatile but near the June baseline, and the full inflationary effect of the shock had yet to emerge.
Another quarter-point increase took the deposit rate to 2.50%, with the staff baseline at 2.5% inflation in 2027. The Council again reserved decisions for each meeting as the outlook evolved.
The Council held the deposit rate at 2.50% as higher energy costs increased inflation risks and weighed on growth. It retained its data-dependent approach without pre-committing to a rate path.

examples.note: At the press conference following a hold, Trichet acknowledged the possibility of an increase at the next meeting. The German two-year yield rose during the conference.

Following another hold, Draghi left the door open to lower rates for an extended period. The two-year yield fell during the conference. Compare this response with the March 2011 conference, another actual hold.

In the decision release, the Council outlined an intended July increase, a further September increase and the end of net asset purchases. Yields already moved in the decision window, before the press conference began.
A quarter-point increase accompanied revised staff inflation projections and an open future rate path. The German two-year yield rose in the decision window.

findings: In the decision-release window the median German two-year yield move was +8.90 bp with tightening guidance (3 releases) and -0.55 bp with easing guidance (3). Among actual holds the medians were +8.90 bp (1) and -0.675 bp (2), respectively.
Conference-window medians were +15.20 bp for tightening (1) and -4.90 bp for easing (1). Each directional group represents a different presidency and calendar date.
The ECB market series used here ends on 2026-06-11. Later selected decisions retain their guidance labels and have an empty market value.
